detail.text: Located on the northern side of the palace's center, the Imperial Domicile was where the emperor lived and conducted his political affairs. In the Latter Naniwa Palace, the Main Hall of the Imperial Domicile was situated in the center of a formal space surrounded by corridors and fences. Excavations revealed that the structure was 26.9 meters wide and 11.9 meters deep. It is thought to have been a high-status structure in a traditional Japanese palace architectural style, with raised floors and pillars embedded directly in the ground, with a Japanese cypress bark-thatched roof, hipped and gabled, surrounded by rims and railings on all four sides.

name: Western Corridor of the Imperial Domicile

detail.text: The Imperial Domicile was where the emperor lived and conducted his political affairs. The central structure was a high-status space surrounded by corridors and walls. The corridor structure was also of high status, consisting of two corridors where people came and went, separated by a central wall with windows.

The Imperial Domicile was where the emperor lived and conducted his political affairs. In the Latter Naniwa Palace it was situated in a separate structure north of the Imperial Audience Hall and State Halls Compound, but in the Former Naniwa Palace, the State Halls Compound occupied a vast space south of the Imperial Domicile South Gate. This main gate was seven pillars (32.7 meters) wide, making it the largest gate among Japan’s ancient palaces. It is thought to have been built in a traditional palace architectural style with a Japanese cypress bark-thatched roof supported by pillars embedded directly in the ground.

The Octagonal Halls stood east and west of the South Gate of the Imperial Domicile. Excavations indicate that the inner pillars were erected using a special method in which one side of the pillar hole was dug out at an angle. As such, it is thought that the halls were multi-storied and nearly 15 meters tall. Opinion differs concerning their purpose, but it is thought that their octagonal design was intended to make the center of the palace more impressive, closely paralleling the Chinese palace construction style.

The Imperial Audience Hall Compound was surrounded by a high-status corridor. Within it stood the Imperial Audience Hall and the Rear Hall, the most important buildings of the Latter Naniwa Palace. The Imperial Audience Hall was built on a stone base and was approximately 42 meters wide and 21 meters deep. The building was roofed with ceramic tiles that were likely painted red, making for a Chinese-style appearance. The roof also featured two types of eaves tiles, Nokimaru and Nokihira. Nokimaru eaves tiles are round and decorated with circular patterns, while Nokihira tiles are flat. During state ceremonies such as the New Year audience, when the emperor would receive greetings from his retainers, as well as when receiving foreign envoys, he would sit on the Takamikura throne in the center of the hall.

name: Rear Hall of the Imperial Audience Hall Compound

detail.text: The Rear Hall of the Imperial Audience Hall was one of the buildings making up the Imperial Audience Hall Compound. It was located on the north side of the compound and connected to the Imperial Audience Hall by a roofed passage between the two buildings. It served as a place for the emperor to rest when using the Imperial Audience Hall for political affairs or ceremonies. The Northern Corridor of the Imperial Audience Hall Compound was attached to both sides of the Rear Hall. The corridor was built on the same site as the Imperial Domicile South Gate of the Former Naniwa Palace. During excavations, traces were found of the removal of tuff used to build the platform of the Rear Hall, along with the pillar holes of the Imperial Domicile South Gate.
